title: The schools, reviewed

cards: A caliph, tradition says, once came to Imam Malik of Medina with an offer. Malik had gathered his book of reports and rulings, the Muwatta.
The caliph wanted copies sent to every province, with orders that everyone follow it and nothing else. One book, one law, no more arguments. Malik turned him down.
The companions of the Prophet, he said, had spread out to many lands, and the people in each place had already heard reports and acted on them. Let them keep what they have.

teach.h: THE PATH, AND THE SCHOLARS' MAP.
teach.b: Start with the path and the map. Shari'ah is the path Allah set. Fiqh is the scholars' understanding of it, human work, done with care.

A school, a madhhab, is a tradition of that understanding, carried from teacher to student. Every school begins with the Qur'an, then the sunnah. Sunni schools add the agreement of scholars and reasoning by likeness.
Ja'fari jurists, followed by Twelver Shia, count reason itself as a source alongside the Qur'an, the sunnah and consensus.

The year walked through the names one by one: Hanafi, from Abu Hanifa in Kufa; Maliki, from Malik in Medina; Shafi'i; Hanbali, from Ahmad ibn Hanbal in Baghdad; Ja'fari, named for Ja'far al-Sadiq; Zaydi, in Yemen; Ibadi, in Oman; and Zahiri, the school of the plain sense.
A statement of scholars called the Amman Message named these eight schools and forbade declaring their followers unbelievers. Why do they differ?
Scholars received different reports, read words in different ways, weighed methods differently, and all of them were seeking the same thing: what Allah asks.
A saying the year met calls that difference a mercy; some attribute it to early scholars rather than to the Prophet.

So when one person in a prayer row folds his hands high and the next folds them low, neither is a mistake waiting to be fixed. Each is a school's careful answer, the kind Malik chose to leave in place.

how: A Muslim may follow one school of law, learned from family, a mosque or a teacher, and Muslims of different schools pray side by side in the same congregation, each following their own school's details.

o: separate religions that grew apart from early Islam
traditions of fiqh, built from the same sources, in one row
buildings where Muslim children learn to recite Qur'an

s: one school is correct and the rest are mistakes
the Amman Message named all eight schools and forbade declaring their followers unbelievers.
Muslims of different schools pray in the same row
they follow one imam, bow together and face one direction.
fiqh and shari'ah mean exactly the same thing
shari'ah is the path Allah set; fiqh is the scholars' human understanding of it.

games.q: you're Malik. the caliph offers to send your book to every province and make everyone follow it. what do you say?
o: yes; one book ends the arguments.
no; people in each place already follow the reports that reached them.
yes, but only in the capital.
games.why: tradition says Malik declined: the companions had spread out, and people had already acted on what reached them.

practice: Bring back Malik's answer, let them keep what they have, and let it settle.
If you pray at a mosque this week, you can stand next to someone whose prayer looks different from yours and simply pray, without a word about it afterward.
If you don't pray, think of one person whose practice differs from yours in a small way, and let it be their careful answer, not a mistake.

wordCard.voice: The schools. Traditions of fiqh, human understanding of the divine law, each built from the same sources and each still standing in the same row. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a school of law, such as the Hanafi or the Ja'fari.

carryVoice: Your line: many schools, one row. Shoulder to shoulder, facing one direction. Same time tomorrow.
